To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the prevalence of HPV infection in cervical cancer in Norway increased from 61% in 1931–1960 to 89% in 1992–2004, and that the HPV type distribution changed over time, from a predominance of HPV 16 in 1931, to an increase in other types in the period 1934–2000.
HPV was detected in a high proportion of neoplastic cervical tissue samples, and that the distribution of HPV subtypes in the samples was different between two 30-year periods.

HPV type 16 is still the most common HPV type in invasive cervical cancers in Norway, but that HPV type 18 has increased in prevalence in Norway, and that HPV types other than 16 and 18 were detected in 33% of the cases in our study.
In summary, our research is concerned with
HPV in cervical cancer and the use of paraffin embedded specimens.
the etiology of cervical cancer in Western Norway, and the study of the HPV subtypes in cervical neoplastic specimens between 1931 to present day.
HPV subtypes in cervical biopsies between the years 1931 and the present.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HPV is an important factor in cervical carcinogenesis, but not the sole cause of the disease.
the HPV 16 is the most common type in Norway, but that the prevalence is decreasing and the number of other types is increasing.
HPV is the most common sexually transmitted disease in the world, with a high incidence of infection in young women.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the HPV type 16 has been the predominant type in Western Norway since the beginning of the 20th century.
HPV is a very common infection and that HPV type 16 is the most prevalent subtype.
we have shown that it is feasible to study HPV subtypes in cervical neoplastic and normal specimens from the early part of the twentieth century.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is feasible to use DNA extracted from formalin fixed and paraffin embedded (FFPE) tissue for molecular studies.
the HPV subtype distribution in cervical cancer has changed during the last 70 years, and that the HPV16 prevalence has been declining.
HPV16 was the only type found during 1930-1934, whereas other HPV subtypes have been detected in one-third of all specimens from 1945 and onward.
